lessons.culture: In Beirut, from a boutique in Hamra to a small neighborhood shop, the seller usually greets you with "ahleen" and brings a few sizes at once. Size words are often borrowed (large, medium, small), and saying something does not fit is normal, never rude.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks you: «شو مقاسك؟» Answer that your size is large.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but a stiff, bookish way to give a clothing size.

exercises.tip: The borrowed English sizes سمول, ميديوم, لارج are what people actually say in shops.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks a woman: «شو مقاسِك؟» Answer that your size is small.

too_formal.feedback: Understandable, but حجم is the size of an object, not a person's clothing size.

exercises.tip: Ask a woman with مقاسِك (kasra at the end); ask a man with مقاسَك.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «بدّي _____ لو سمحت.» English meaning: I want a shirt, please.

too_formal.feedback: A roundabout, formal way to describe a shirt; the everyday word is simply قميص.

exercises.tip: بدّي plus the item name is the everyday way to ask for something in a shop.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «هيدا كتير _____ عليّي.» English meaning: This is too big for me.

too_formal.feedback: This sounds like a description of a room, not clothing that does not fit.

exercises.tip: كتير + adjective + عليّي is the everyday pattern for "too X for me".

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "Can I try it on?"

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine, but this is Modern Standard Arabic, not how it is said in a shop.

exercises.tip: فيني is "can I" in everyday Lebanese speech.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "Where's the fitting room?"

too_formal.feedback: The meaning is right, but أين and the fuller phrasing are formal; Lebanese say وين.

exercises.tip: وين replaces أين everywhere in Lebanese speech.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "too tight"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but كتير is what is said for "too"/"very", not جدا.

exercises.tip: ضيّق is tight, the opposite of واسع (loose, wide).

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Do you have a smaller size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning but far too formal, like a customer-service script.

exercises.tip: عندك (do you have) opens a question about what is available.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This is too big for me."

too_formal.feedback: Correct Arabic, but هذا and جدا are the written forms, not the spoken ones.

exercises.tip: هيدا (this) opens the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "Do you have a bigger size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but هل لديك is the written way to ask.

exercises.tip: عندك opens a question about what is available.

I recommend the black, it looks great on you.

pair.english: Which is nicer, red or blue?

response.english: Blue is nicer in my opinion.

lessons.culture: Sellers in Lebanese shops like to help you choose, often bringing out a few colors unasked and giving an honest opinion. Saying a color does not suit you is heard as useful, not rude.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks: «شو رأيك بهالفستان؟» Say it is very nice.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this bookish phrasing is not how anyone reacts to a dress in a shop.

exercises.tip: حلو (nice, pretty) is the everyday word of approval for almost anything.

exercises.prompt: The shopkeeper asks: «شو بتنصحني آخد؟» Recommend the black one and say it looks great on them.

too_formal.item: أنصحك باللون الأسود لأنه يليق بك
too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but far more formal than the quick, casual way a shopkeeper gives advice.

exercises.tip: حلو عليك (it looks good on you) is the natural compliment, dropped in casually.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «عاجبني اللون _____.» English meaning: I like the blue color.

too_formal.feedback: Over-specified; nobody adds "sky-blue" unless they mean a very particular shade.

exercises.tip: Colors take ال (the) when naming a specific one you like.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «هيدا كتير _____ عليّي.» English meaning: This is too dark for me.

too_formal.feedback: An exaggerated, literary way to describe a shade; غامق alone is what is said.

exercises.tip: غامق (dark) pairs with فاتح (light) for describing shades.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "Do you have another color?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but far too formal, like a customer-service script rather than a shop chat.

exercises.tip: تاني is "other, another", used constantly in daily speech.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "I haven't decided yet."

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff; لسّا (not yet) is the spoken word, never لم ... بعد in conversation.

exercises.tip: لسّا ما + verb is the everyday way to say "haven't yet".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "light" (a light color)?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but wordier than needed.

exercises.tip: فاتح is light, pale; its opposite is غامق (dark).

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Just give me this one"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but أعطني and فقط are the written forms.

exercises.tip: عطيني (give me) is how a shopper asks to be handed an item.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This color doesn't suit me."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but this is the written way to say it.

exercises.tip: مش (not) sits right before the word it negates.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "Which is nicer, red or blue?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; أيهما ... أم is the written pattern.

exercises.tip: ولّا links the two choices in an either/or question.

lessons.culture: Bargaining is normal in Beirut's small shops and street stalls, less so in chain stores where prices are fixed. A first price is often an opening one, and a friendly back and forth is expected. Prices may be quoted in US dollars or in Lebanese lira, so listen for which one.

exercises.prompt: You ask «قدّيش هيدا؟» and the shopkeeper waits. Say it is very expensive.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine, but this is how a news item would phrase it, not a shopper reacting out loud.

exercises.tip: غالي (expensive) is the blunt, everyday reaction to a high price.

exercises.prompt: You and the shopkeeper agree on a price. Say "Ok, we agreed."

too_formal.feedback: Correct but sounds like closing a business contract, not a friendly handshake over a shirt.

exercises.tip: متفقين (agreed) closes a bargain warmly and simply.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «_____ هيدا؟» English meaning: How much is this?

too_formal.feedback: Overly wordy; the one word قدّيش already means "how much".

exercises.tip: قدّيش alone asks about price, quantity or amount; بكم also works for prices.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «هيدا _____ سعر.» English meaning: This is the final price.

too_formal.item: السعر النهائي والأخير الذي لا يمكن تجاوزه
too_formal.feedback: Way too elaborate; a shopkeeper just says آخر سعر and means it.

exercises.tip: آخر سعر (final price) is the standard way to end haggling; آخر كلمة is also heard.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "Can you lower the price?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is how a formal request would be written, not asked across a counter.

exercises.tip: فيك (can you) plus تنزّل السعر (lower the price) is the everyday ask.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "Isn't there cheaper than this?"

too_formal.item: ألا يوجد شيء أرخص من هذا؟
too_formal.feedback: Correct but stilted; the spoken form goes straight to ما في.

exercises.tip: ما في is "there isn't"; هيك is "like this, than this".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "expensive"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but bookish; غالي is what is said.

exercises.tip: غالي is expensive; its opposite is رخيص (cheap).

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Lower it a bit for me"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this sounds like a written request.

exercises.tip: نزّلّي (lower for me) plus شوي (a little) softens the ask.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "I want a discount because I'm buying a lot."
exercises.answer: بدّي خصم لأني عم اشتري كتير

too_formal.feedback: Correct Arabic, but no one bargains in the written register.

exercises.tip: عم + verb says "I'm buying" as it happens; لأني links the reason to the request.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "How much did the total come to?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; كم بلغ is the written phrasing.

exercises.tip: صار (became, came to) is used for a total reached after adding up.

pair.english: I want to return this shirt.

response.english: No, but I can exchange it for you.

pair.english: Can I exchange it for a bigger size?

lessons.culture: Many Lebanese shops prefer to exchange an item or give store credit rather than refund cash, especially on sale items, so keep the receipt. A real defect is usually accepted without an argument.

exercises.prompt: The shopkeeper asks: «شو المشكلة؟» Say there is a defect.

too_formal.feedback: Overly technical; a customer just says فيه عيب and points to it.

exercises.tip: فيه عيب (there's a defect) is enough, the shopkeeper will ask to see it.

exercises.prompt: The shop only exchanges, it does not refund. Ask: "Can I exchange it for a bigger size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is how a written complaint form would phrase it.

exercises.tip: فيني بدّلو (can I exchange it) is the direct spoken ask.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «معي _____.» English meaning: I have the receipt.

too_formal.feedback: Nobody in a shop calls it the "official purchase receipt"; it is just الفاتورة.

exercises.tip: الفاتورة is the everyday word for a receipt or invoice.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: «هيدا مش المقاس _____.» English meaning: This is the wrong size.

too_formal.feedback: Far too wordy; مش المقاس الصح is what is said.

exercises.tip: الصح (the right one) is the spoken word; مش negates it to mean "the wrong one".

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "I want to return this shirt."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is formal phrasing, not what is said walking up to the counter.

exercises.tip: بدّي رجّع (I want to return) opens the request plainly.

exercises.prompt: Say in Lebanese: "When did you buy it?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff, sounds like a form question rather than a shopkeeper asking casually.

exercises.tip: إيمتى (when) is the spoken word; شريتو is a common short form of اشتريتو.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "a defect"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but technical; عيب is the everyday word.

exercises.tip: عيب covers a flaw in an object, and also means "shameful" for behavior.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I don't have the receipt"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; ليس معي is the written form.

exercises.tip: ما معي (I don't have on me) negates معي (I have on me).

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This isn't what I ordered."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but ليس ما is the written pattern.

exercises.tip: يلّي (that which) introduces what was ordered.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "I want to exchange it for another one."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but formal and written.

exercises.tip: بغيرو (for another one of it) follows the verb بدّلو (exchange it).

challenge.title: A Shopping Trip in Beirut
challenge.instructions: Write and act a shopping conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include asking for an item by size, discussing a color choice, checking the price, bargaining at least once, and a return or exchange with the receipt mentioned. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 6 and include both a masculine-address and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: An opening request using بدّي and a clothing item.
A size question using شو مقاسك؟ or شو مقاسِك؟
A color question or preference using اللون.
At least one bargaining line using فيك تنزّل السعر؟ or نزّلّي شوي.
A final price line using آخر سعر.
A return or exchange line using بدّي رجّع or بدّي بدّلو.
A mention of the receipt using الفاتورة.
A closing thank-you or blessing such as يسلمو or الله يخلّيك.
